lessons.title: Get ready! What you will learn

pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 💻 **Strand 1 — Introduction To Computing**
Sub-strand 1: Components of Computers and Computer Systems

Every time you send a WhatsApp message, pay with Mobile Money or watch a video, millions of tiny electronic switches work together inside a computer. In this unit you will look inside the modern computer. You will meet the microprocessor that started the fourth generation of computers, the devices we use to put data in and get information out, and the drives that store our work. You will also learn to manage the Windows desktop and organise your files like a professional.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B7.1.1.1** Examine the parts of a computer.
- **B7.1.1.2** Demonstrate the use of the features of the Windows Desktop.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B7.1.1.1.1** Discuss the fourth-generation computers.
- **B7.1.1.1.2** Demonstrate understanding in the use of input devices (barcode, scanner, etc.).
- **B7.1.1.1.3** Examine the uses of the output devices: graphing plotter, data and multimedia projectors as well as pico projector.
- **B7.1.1.1.4** Examine full-sized external hard drives, hard drive speed, disk caching, portable hard drives, optical discs and drives.
- **B7.1.1.2.1** Discover the latest Windows Operating System (Start screen, tiles, taskbar buttons, preview thumbnails, peeking).
- **B7.1.1.2.2** Practise file management techniques (file & folder management, users & accounts).

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 1.1 Fourth-Generation Computers
- 1.2 Input Devices
- 1.3 Output Devices: Plotters and Projectors
- 1.4 Hard Drives and Optical Storage
- 1.5 Exploring the Windows Desktop
- 1.6 File Management, Users and Accounts

**Core competencies developed:** Creativity and Innovation (CI), Communication and Collaboration (CC), Digital Literacy (DL), Critical Thinking and Problem Solving (CP), Cultural Identity and Global Citizenship (CG), Personal Development and Leadership (PL).

lessons.title: Fourth-Generation Computers

pages.title: Fourth-Generation Computers
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe the main features of fourth-generation computers;
- identify a microchip and explain what it does;
- explain the basic architecture of a processor (CU, ALU, registers, cache and buses).
Computers have changed a great deal since the first electronic machines were built in the 1940s. Historians group these changes into **generations**. Each generation began when a new electronic technology made computers smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable.
[[fig:c7-f02|Figure 1: The five generations of computers]]
## What makes a computer “fourth generation”?
The fourth generation began in **1971**, when the American company Intel released the **Intel 4004**, the first commercially available **microprocessor**. A microprocessor places the whole Central Processing Unit (CPU) of a computer on a single silicon chip. This was possible because of **Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI)**, a manufacturing method that packs thousands, and today billions, of transistors onto one chip.
Almost every computer you will use, including desktop PCs, laptops, tablets, smartphones, smart TVs, ATMs and the computer inside a car, belongs to the fourth generation.

pages.title: Features of fourth-generation computers
pages.body:
## Features of fourth-generation computers
| **Feature** | **What it means for users** |
|---|---|
| Microprocessor (VLSI) technology | The entire CPU fits on one chip, so computers became small enough to sit on a desk, rest on a lap or fit in a pocket. |
| Very high speed | Modern processors carry out billions of instructions every second. Speed is measured in gigahertz (GHz). |
| Large memory and storage | Semiconductor RAM replaced older magnetic-core memory. Storage grew from kilobytes to terabytes. |
| Small size and low cost | Personal computers (PCs) became affordable for homes, schools and small businesses. The IBM PC (1981) and Apple Macintosh (1984) are famous early examples. |
| Less heat and power use | Far less heat than the vacuum tubes and early transistors; fans or heat sinks are usually enough to cool them. |
| Graphical User Interface (GUI) | Users click icons, windows and menus with a mouse or touch the screen, instead of typing commands. |
| Networking and the Internet | Computers can share files, printers and information through networks and the Internet. |
| High-level programming languages | Languages such as C, C++, Java and Python make programming easier. |
| Reliability and portability | Fewer moving parts and better chips mean fewer breakdowns; batteries allow mobile use. |

pages.title: Features of fourth-generation computers (continued)
pages.body:
> ✨ **Did you know? — From a room to your pocket** ENIAC (1946), a first-generation computer, weighed about 27 tonnes and filled a large room. A modern smartphone weighs under 200 g but is millions of times more powerful.
## Identifying a microchip
A **microchip** (also called a **chip** or **integrated circuit, IC**) is a tiny slice of **silicon** on which millions or billions of microscopic electronic components (mainly transistors) are built. The chip is sealed in a protective plastic or ceramic package with metal **pins** or contact pads that connect it to the **motherboard**.
[[fig:c7-f03|Figure 2: Parts of a microchip]]
Chips are found on the motherboard of every computer. Common chips include:
- **The microprocessor (CPU):** the “brain” that carries out instructions. It usually sits in a square socket under a heat sink and fan.
- **Memory chips (RAM):** on long, thin circuit boards called memory modules.
- **The BIOS/UEFI chip:** stores the start-up instructions the computer needs when it is switched on.
- **Chipset, graphics and network chips:** control communication between parts and handle pictures and networking.
- **Chips in everyday items:** SIM cards, bank cards, mobile phones, digital watches, calculators and modern cars.
> 🛡️ **Safety first** Never touch the pins of a chip with bare fingers or remove chips from a working computer. Static electricity from your body can destroy them. Technicians wear an **anti-static wrist strap**, and you should only open a computer under your teacher’s supervision.

pages.title: Exploring the architecture of a processor
pages.body:
## Exploring the architecture of a processor
The **architecture** of a processor is the way its parts are organised and connected. Most computers follow the **von Neumann architecture**: programs and data are both kept in memory, and the CPU fetches them one at a time.
[[fig:c7-f04|Figure 3: The main parts of the CPU and how data moves through the computer]]
| **Part** | **Job** |
|---|---|
| Control Unit (CU) | Directs all operations. It fetches each instruction from memory, decodes it, and sends control signals to the other parts telling them what to do. It works like the conductor of a choir or a traffic warden. |
| Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) | Carries out arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and logical operations (comparisons such as “is A greater than B?”, and AND, OR, NOT). |
| Registers | Very small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU that hold the data and instructions being worked on at that instant (e.g. the Program Counter holds the address of the next instruction). |
| Cache memory | Fast memory on or near the CPU that keeps copies of frequently used data so the CPU does not wait for slower RAM. Levels: L1 (smallest, fastest), L2, L3 (larger, slower). |
| Buses | Electrical pathways that carry data (data bus), memory locations (address bus) and control signals (control bus) between the CPU, memory and devices. |
| Clock | Sends regular pulses that keep all operations in step. Clock speed is measured in hertz (Hz); 3.5 GHz = 3.5 billion cycles per second. |
| Cores | A modern processor contains several cores, each a complete processing unit, so it can work on several tasks at the same time (dual-core, quad-core, octa-core). |

pages.title: Exploring the architecture of a processor (continued)
pages.body:
**The fetch–decode–execute cycle**
The CPU repeats the same three steps billions of times per second:
1. **Fetch:** the CU collects the next instruction from memory.
2. **Decode:** the CU works out what the instruction means.
3. **Execute:** the ALU or another part carries out the instruction, and the result is stored in a register or in memory.
> ⏳ **Then and now — WHAT YOU WILL SEE TODAY** Desktop and laptop processors today come mainly from **Intel** (Core Ultra, Core i3/i5/i7/i9) and **AMD** (Ryzen). Phones and many new laptops use processors based on **ARM** designs, such as Qualcomm Snapdragon, Apple M-series and MediaTek chips. You can see your own processor in Windows: **Settings › System › About**, or press **Ctrl + Shift + Esc** to open Task Manager and choose **Performance › CPU**.
> 🧪 **Activity — Investigate your school computer**
1. Open **Settings › System › About** on a lab computer. Write down the processor name, its speed (GHz) and the installed RAM.
2. Open Task Manager (**Ctrl + Shift + Esc**) › **Performance**. Count the number of cores and note the sizes of the L1, L2 and L3 caches.
3. In groups, compare your findings and present a short report to the class explaining what each value means.

pages.title: Input Devices
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- identify common input devices such as the wireless keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, barcode reader and scanner;
- demonstrate the correct use of input devices;
- distinguish between manual and automatic input devices;
- state advantages, disadvantages and areas of use of input devices.
An **input device** is any hardware used to enter data or instructions into a computer. Input is the first stage of the **Input → Process → Output** cycle (with **Storage** keeping data for later use).
[[fig:c7-f05|Figure 4: Manual and automatic input devices]]
## Manual and automatic input
**Manual input devices** need a person to enter each piece of data by hand, for example by pressing keys, moving a mouse or touching a screen. **Automatic input devices** (also called **direct data entry** devices) read data straight from its source, such as a barcode, a printed page or a card, with little human effort. They are faster and make fewer mistakes when large amounts of data must be captured.
## Common input devices
**Keyboard (wired and wireless)**
The keyboard is used to type text, numbers and commands. A **wireless keyboard** connects by **Bluetooth** or by a small **USB radio receiver (dongle)** instead of a cable, which keeps desks tidy and lets you type from a distance (for example, to control a presentation). It needs batteries or charging.

pages.title: Input Devices (continued)
pages.body:
**Mouse and touchpad**
A mouse moves the on-screen pointer. Modern mice are **optical** (they use an LED and a tiny camera to track movement). The basic mouse actions are: **click** (select), **double-click** (open), **right-click** (shortcut menu), **drag and drop** (move), and **scroll** (move up/down a page). Laptops use a **touchpad** in place of a mouse.
**Touchscreen**
A touchscreen is both an input and an output device: you touch the display to select, swipe, pinch to zoom or type on an on-screen keyboard. Smartphones use **capacitive** touchscreens that sense the electrical charge in your finger; some ATMs and older devices use **resistive** screens that respond to pressure.
**Barcode reader (scanner)**
A barcode reader shines light (usually a laser or LED) across a **barcode**, a pattern of black and white bars that represents a number. The reader measures the reflected light and sends the number to the computer, which looks up the product name and price. Barcode readers are used at supermarket checkouts, in libraries, warehouses, hospitals (patient wristbands) and on examination answer scripts.
**Scanner**
A scanner converts printed documents and photographs into digital images. A **flatbed scanner** has a glass surface on which you place the page; a **sheet-fed (document) scanner** pulls pages through automatically; a **handheld scanner** is moved across the page. With **OCR (Optical Character Recognition)** software, scanned text can be turned into editable text.

pages.title: Input Devices (continued)
pages.body:
> 🪜 **Step by step — Scanning a document with a flatbed scanner**
1. Switch on the scanner and make sure it is connected to the computer.
2. Lift the lid and place the document **face down** on the glass, aligned with the corner arrow.
3. On the computer, open **Windows Scan** (or the scanner’s own software). Choose the scanner, then select the file type (e.g. **PNG** or **PDF**) and the colour mode.
4. Click **Preview**, adjust the area to scan if necessary, then click **Scan**.
5. Save the file with a meaningful name in the correct folder (e.g. Documents\School\Science\Scanned_Notes_2026-11-17.pdf).
## Advantages and disadvantages of input devices
| **Device** | **Advantages** | **Disadvantages** | **Where used** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keyboard | Accurate for entering text and numbers; familiar; cheap | Slow for large data; can cause RSI with long use | Offices, schools, typing reports |
| Wireless keyboard/mouse | No cable clutter; can be used from a distance | Batteries run down; possible interference or delay | Presentations, home theatre PCs |
| Mouse | Fast for pointing and selecting; easy to learn | Needs a flat surface; not good for typing text | All desktop computers |
| Touchscreen | Very easy and natural; no extra devices needed | Screen gets dirty; finger can hide small items; less precise | Phones, tablets, ATMs, ticket machines |
| Barcode reader | Very fast and accurate; reduces human error | Damaged/dirty barcodes may not scan; only reads codes | Supermarkets, libraries, warehouses |
| Scanner | Quickly digitises documents and photos; OCR saves retyping | Image quality depends on the original; large files | Offices, archives, schools |

pages.title: Input Devices (continued)
pages.body:
> 💻 **Practical session — Using input devices in the lab**
1. Type a short paragraph about your hometown using the keyboard. Practise using **Shift**, **Caps Lock**, **Backspace**, **Delete** and **Enter**.
2. Use the mouse to click, double-click, right-click, drag a file into a folder and scroll through a web page.
3. If available, scan your class timetable, or use a phone camera app to scan a barcode or QR code. Record what information was captured.
4. Discuss: which devices you used were manual, and which were automatic?

lessons.title: Output Devices: Plotters and Projectors

pages.title: Output Devices: Plotters and Projectors
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe the graphing plotter, data projector, multimedia projector and pico projector;
- demonstrate how to set up and use a projector;
- state the advantages and disadvantages of these output devices.
An **output device** presents the results of processing in a form people can use: on paper (**hard copy**), on a screen (**soft copy**), or as sound. This lesson focuses on devices for large drawings and large audiences.
## Graphing plotter
A **plotter** produces very large, high-quality line drawings such as building plans, maps, engineering designs, banners and charts. Traditional **pen plotters** moved coloured pens across the paper to draw continuous lines. Modern **wide-format (large-format) plotters** use inkjet technology and print on paper rolls up to about 1.5 m wide.
- **Flatbed plotter:** paper lies flat while the pen moves in two directions.
- **Drum plotter:** paper is wrapped around a rotating drum while the pen moves across it.
- **Cutting plotter (vinyl cutter):** uses a blade instead of a pen to cut shapes for signs and stickers.
## Data projector
A **data projector** connects to a computer or laptop and projects what is on the screen onto a wall or projection screen so a whole class or audience can see it. Two common technologies are **LCD** (light passes through liquid-crystal panels) and **DLP** (light reflects off millions of tiny mirrors on a chip).

pages.title: Output Devices: Plotters and Projectors (continued)
pages.body:
When choosing a projector, check its **brightness** in **lumens** (classrooms usually need about 3,000 lumens or more), its **resolution** (e.g. 1920 × 1080 Full HD) and its **connections** (HDMI, VGA, USB, wireless screen-mirroring).
## Multimedia projector
A **multimedia projector** is a data projector with extra features for audio and video: built-in **speakers**, the ability to play videos, pictures and slides directly from a **USB flash drive** or **memory card**, and sometimes Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and a built-in operating system. Schools, churches and event centres use them for films, presentations and worship lyrics.
## Pico projector
A **pico projector** (pocket or mini projector) is a very small, battery-powered projector that fits in a hand or pocket. Some are built into smartphones or cameras. They are ideal for showing slides to a small group anywhere, but their brightness is low, so the room must be dark and the picture small.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Setting up a projector for a class presentation**
1. Place the projector on a stable table or confirm the ceiling mount is secure. Keep cables taped down or away from walkways.
2. Connect the projector to the laptop with an **HDMI** (or VGA) cable, then connect the power cable and switch on the projector.
3. Switch on the laptop. If the picture does not appear, press **Windows key + P** and choose **Duplicate** (same image on both screens) or **Extend**.
4. Adjust the **focus** and **zoom** rings until the text is sharp, and use **keystone** correction if the picture looks like a trapezium.
5. After use, switch off the projector and allow the cooling fan to stop before unplugging, to protect the lamp.

pages.title: Output Devices: Plotters and Projectors (continued)
pages.body:
> 🛡️ **Safety first** Never look directly into the projector lens when it is on. The bright light can damage your eyes.
| **Device** | **Advantages** | **Disadvantages** |
|---|---|---|
| Graphing plotter | Very large, precise drawings; continuous lines; prints on many materials | Expensive; large; slower than printers; not suited to everyday text |
| Data projector | Whole class sees the same image; supports teaching and meetings | Needs a darkened room; lamps are costly to replace; needs power |
| Multimedia projector | Plays media without a computer; built-in sound | More expensive; built-in speakers are often weak for large halls |
| Pico projector | Very portable; battery-powered; cheap to run | Low brightness and small image; short battery life |
> 🇬🇭 **Ghana connection** Many Ghanaian classrooms without enough computers use one laptop and a projector so that every learner can follow a computing demonstration. When a projector is not available, your teacher may use clear pictures, printed screenshots or improvised models, as the curriculum recommends.

pages.title: Hard Drives and Optical Storage
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.1.4
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- identify magnetic storage devices, portable hard drives, optical discs and drives;
- describe the features of hard drives and optical discs;
- compare the maximum capacities and write speeds of storage media;
- explain hard drive speed and disk caching, and the differences between types of hard disk drive.
**Storage devices** keep data and programs permanently, even when the computer is switched off. RAM is temporary (volatile) memory, so anything you have not saved is lost when the power goes off. Storage is measured in bytes:
| **Unit** | **Size** | **Roughly holds** |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Byte (B) | 8 bits | one character, e.g. the letter A |
| 1 Kilobyte (KB) | 1,024 bytes | a short paragraph |
| 1 Megabyte (MB) | 1,024 KB | a one-minute MP3 song is about 1 MB |
| 1 Gigabyte (GB) | 1,024 MB | about 250 songs or a short HD film |
| 1 Terabyte (TB) | 1,024 GB | about 250,000 photos |
> 🎯 **BECE focus** Learn the order of storage units: **bit → byte → KB → MB → GB → TB → PB**. In computing, each unit is 1,024 times the one before it, although drive manufacturers often round to 1,000.
## Magnetic storage: the hard disk drive (HDD)
A **hard disk drive** stores data magnetically on spinning metal or glass disks called **platters**. A **read/write head** on a moving **actuator arm** floats just above each platter to record and read the magnetic patterns. Data is organised in circular **tracks** divided into **sectors**.

pages.title: Hard Drives and Optical Storage (continued)
pages.body:
[[fig:c7-f06|Figure 5: The main parts of a hard disk drive]]
## Types of hard disk drive
| **Type** | **Features** | **Typical capacity (2026)** |
|---|---|---|
| Internal desktop HDD (3.5-inch) | Fitted inside a desktop computer and connected with a SATA cable; powered by the computer | 1 TB – 24 TB+ |
| Internal laptop HDD (2.5-inch) | Smaller and uses less power; fits inside laptops | 500 GB – 5 TB |
| Full-sized external hard drive | A 3.5-inch drive in its own case; connects by USB or Thunderbolt; needs its own **mains power adapter**; used for backups and large media libraries | 4 TB – 24 TB+ |
| Portable hard drive | A 2.5-inch drive in a small case; powered through the USB cable, so no adapter is needed; easy to carry | 1 TB – 5 TB |
**Hard drive speed**
Hard drive performance depends on:
- **Rotational speed:** measured in **revolutions per minute (rpm)**. Common speeds are 5,400 rpm (laptops, portable drives), 7,200 rpm (desktops) and 10,000–15,000 rpm (servers). The faster the platters spin, the sooner the data reaches the head.
- **Seek time / access time:** how long the head takes to move to the right track, measured in milliseconds (ms).
- **Data transfer rate:** how many megabytes per second (MB/s) can be read or written. Typical HDDs transfer about 100–250 MB/s.
- **Interface:** the connection type. Internal drives use **SATA** (up to 6 Gb/s); external drives use **USB 3.x** or **USB-C/Thunderbolt**. An old USB 2.0 port limits the speed to about 35–40 MB/s.

pages.title: Hard Drives and Optical Storage (continued)
pages.body:
**Disk caching**
**Disk caching** speeds up a hard drive by keeping recently used or soon-needed data in fast memory. Every hard drive has a small built-in **buffer (cache)** of RAM, typically 64–256 MB. The operating system also uses part of the main RAM as a disk cache. When the CPU asks for data that is already in the cache (a **cache hit**), it is delivered almost instantly instead of waiting for the platters to spin.
> ✨ **Did you know?** Think of disk caching like keeping your most-used exercise books in your school bag rather than in your locker. You reach them faster because they are close at hand.
## Optical discs and drives
**Optical discs** store data as microscopic **pits** and flat areas (**lands**) on a reflective layer. A **laser** in the optical drive reads the disc by detecting how light is reflected. CDs use an infrared laser, DVDs a red laser and Blu-ray discs a **blue-violet laser**, whose shorter wavelength allows smaller pits and therefore much more data.
| **Category** | **Examples** | **What you can do** |
|---|---|---|
| Read-only (ROM) | CD-ROM, DVD-ROM, BD-ROM | Data is pressed at the factory. You can read it but cannot change it (e.g. software installation discs, films). |
| Recordable (R) | CD-R, DVD-R, DVD+R, BD-R | Write once, read many times (WORM). Data cannot be erased once recorded. |
| Rewritable (RW/RE) | CD-RW, DVD-RW, DVD+RW, BD-RE | Can be written, erased and rewritten many times (about 1,000 times for CD-RW). |

pages.title: Hard Drives and Optical Storage (continued)
pages.body:
**DVD-R and DVD+R** are two competing recordable formats developed by different groups of companies. Most modern DVD writers (marked “DVD±RW”) can use both.
[[fig:c7-f07|Figure 6: Maximum capacities of common storage media]]
**Capacities and write speeds**
| **Disc** | **Maximum capacity** | **Base speed (1×)** | **Typical maximum write speed** |
|---|---|---|---|
| CD-R / CD-RW | 650–700 MB (about 80 minutes of audio) | 150 KB/s | 52× ≈ 7.8 MB/s (CD-RW slower, about 24×) |
| DVD±R / DVD±RW | 4.7 GB single layer; 8.5 GB dual layer | 1.385 MB/s | 24× ≈ 33 MB/s (RW about 6–8×) |
| BD-R / BD-RE | 25 GB single layer; 50 GB dual layer; 100–128 GB BDXL | 4.5 MB/s | 16× ≈ 72 MB/s (BD-RE about 2×) |
> ✏️ **Worked example — How many CDs equal one DVD?**
A single-layer DVD holds 4.7 GB. A CD holds 700 MB = 0.7 GB (approximately).
Number of CDs = 4.7 ÷ 0.7 ≈ **6.7**, so the data on one DVD would need about **7 CDs**.
> ⏳ **Then and now — WHAT YOU WILL SEE TODAY** Most new laptops no longer have a built-in optical drive. People now use **USB flash drives**, **SSDs** and **cloud storage** (you will study these in Basic 8 and 9). Optical discs are still used for films, game consoles, music albums and long-term archives, and an **external USB DVD/Blu-ray drive** can be connected when needed.
> 🧪 **Activity — Storage show-and-tell**
In groups, collect real storage devices or pictures of them (old CDs, DVDs, a hard drive, a portable drive). Label each with its type, capacity and whether it is magnetic or optical. Present a table comparing their capacity, speed, portability and cost.

lessons.title: Exploring the Windows Desktop

pages.title: Exploring the Windows Desktop
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.2.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- identify the desktop, Start menu/screen, tiles and taskbar;
- preview windows using taskbar thumbnails;
- temporarily “peek” at a window or the desktop from the taskbar.
An **operating system (OS)** is the system software that manages the computer’s hardware and lets you run programs. **Microsoft Windows** is the most widely used desktop OS. The **desktop** is the main screen you see after you sign in. It is your work area.
[[fig:c7-f08|Figure 7: Features of the Windows desktop and taskbar]]
## The Start screen and tiles
Clicking the **Start** button (or pressing the **Windows key**) opens the Start menu. In **Windows 8**, Start opened a full **Start screen** made of coloured rectangles called **tiles**. In **Windows 10**, the Start menu shows **live tiles** that can display changing information, such as weather or news headlines. Tiles can be resized, moved and grouped.
> ⏳ **Then and now — WHAT YOU WILL SEE TODAY Windows 11** **Windows 11** is the current version of Windows. Microsoft ended support for Windows 10 on 14 October 2025. In Windows 11, the Start menu replaces tiles with a grid of **pinned app icons**, a **Recommended** section and an **All apps** list. To pin an app, right-click it and choose **Pin to Start**. The ideas you learn here (opening apps from Start, pinning and arranging them) work the same way.

pages.title: The taskbar and its buttons
pages.body:
## The taskbar and its buttons
The **taskbar** is the bar along the bottom of the screen. It contains:
- **Start button**: opens the Start menu.
- **Search**: find apps, files and settings by typing their name.
- **Task View**: shows all open windows and virtual desktops (**Windows key + Tab**).
- **Pinned and running app buttons**: a line under a button shows the app is open.
- **Notification area (system tray)**: shows network, volume and battery icons, and the date and time.
## Preview thumbnails and peeking
When several windows are open, hovering the mouse pointer over an app’s taskbar button shows a small **preview thumbnail** of each of its open windows. Hovering over a thumbnail lets you **peek**: the full window is shown temporarily, and all other windows become transparent. Move the pointer away and the screen returns to normal; click the thumbnail to switch to that window.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Previewing and peeking at windows**
1. Open three programs, for example File Explorer, Word and a web browser.
2. Hover (do not click) over the **Word** button on the taskbar. A preview thumbnail appears.
3. Move the pointer onto the thumbnail. Word appears full size while the other windows fade: this is a temporary peek.
4. Move the pointer away to return to your previous view, or click the thumbnail to switch to Word.
5. To peek at the desktop, point to the **far right corner** of the taskbar. (In Windows 11, turn this on in **Settings › Personalisation › Taskbar › Taskbar behaviours › “Select the far corner of the taskbar to show the desktop”**.) You can also press **Windows key + , (comma)** to peek, or **Windows key + D** to show the desktop.

pages.title: The taskbar and its buttons (continued)
pages.body:
| **Shortcut** | **Action** |
|---|---|
| Windows key | Open or close Start |
| Windows + D | Show or hide the desktop |
| Windows + E | Open File Explorer |
| Alt + Tab | Switch between open windows |
| Windows + Tab | Open Task View |
| Windows + L | Lock the computer |

pages.title: File Management, Users and Accounts
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.1.1.2.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- create, name, organise, copy, move and delete files and folders using naming conventions;
- explain the types and importance of file extensions;
- describe different account levels for users of a computer;
- explain the permission levels that apply to files and folders.
A **file** is a collection of data saved with a name, such as an essay, a photo or a song. A **folder** (directory) is a container used to group related files and other folders (**sub-folders**). **File management** means organising files so you can find, protect and back them up easily.
[[fig:c7-f09|Figure 8: A well-organised folder structure]]
## File naming conventions
A **naming convention** is an agreed set of rules for naming files. Good names tell you what is inside a file without opening it.
- Use short but **meaningful** names, e.g. B7_Science_Photosynthesis_Notes.docx, not New Document (3).docx.
- Write dates as **YYYY-MM-DD** (e.g. 2026-11-17) so files sort in date order.
- Use underscores _ or hyphens - instead of spaces when sharing files online.
- Add version numbers when you revise work: Essay_v1, Essay_v2, Essay_Final.
- Windows does **not** allow these characters in names: \ / : ∗ ? " < > |.
- Do not change or delete the **extension** (the part after the last dot).

pages.title: File Management, Users and Accounts (continued)
pages.body:
> 🪜 **Step by step — Creating and organising folders in File Explorer**
1. Press **Windows key + E** to open File Explorer and open **Documents**.
2. Click **New › Folder** (or press **Ctrl + Shift + N**). Type School_2026 and press **Enter**.
3. Open the new folder and create sub-folders named Computing, Mathematics and Science.
4. To **rename** a file or folder, select it and press **F2**, type the new name and press **Enter**.
5. To **copy**: select the file, press **Ctrl + C**, open the destination folder and press **Ctrl + V**. To **move**: use **Ctrl + X** then **Ctrl + V**, or drag and drop.
6. To **delete**, select the item and press **Delete**. It goes to the **Recycle Bin**, from which it can be restored. **Shift + Delete** removes it permanently, so use it with care.
## File extensions
A **file extension** is the group of letters after the last dot in a file name (for example, .docx in Report.docx). It tells Windows the **file type** and which program should open it. Windows hides extensions by default. To show them, open File Explorer and choose **View › Show › File name extensions** (Windows 11) or tick **File name extensions** on the **View** tab (Windows 10).

pages.title: File Management, Users and Accounts (continued)
pages.body:
| **Extension** | **File type** | **Opens with (example)** |
|---|---|---|
| .docx / .doc | Word document | Microsoft Word, LibreOffice Writer |
| .xlsx / .xls | Spreadsheet workbook | Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc |
| .pptx / .ppt | Presentation | Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides |
| .pdf | Portable Document Format | Microsoft Edge, Adobe Acrobat Reader |
| .txt | Plain text | Notepad |
| .jpg / .png / .gif | Images | Photos app, Paint |
| .mp3 / .wav | Audio | Media Player |
| .mp4 / .avi | Video | Media Player, VLC |
| .zip | Compressed folder | File Explorer, 7-Zip |
| .exe / .msi | Program / installer | Runs as a program |
| .html | Web page | Web browser |
| .py / .sb3 | Python program / Scratch 3 project | Python IDLE / Scratch |
> 🛡️ **Safety first — Beware of double extensions** Criminals sometimes disguise harmful programs with names like Results.pdf.exe. With extensions hidden, it looks like Results.pdf. Showing file extensions helps you spot this trick. Never open unexpected .exe files received by email or WhatsApp.
## User accounts and account levels
A **user account** is a record that identifies a person to the computer, with a **user name**, **password** (or PIN), personal files and settings. Accounts let several people share one computer safely.

pages.title: File Management, Users and Accounts (continued)
pages.body:
| **Account level** | **What the user can do** | **Who should use it** |
|---|---|---|
| Administrator | Full control: install and remove programs, change system settings, create or delete accounts, access all files. | The ICT teacher or lab technician |
| Standard user | Use programs and their own files; change personal settings. Must enter an administrator password to make system-wide changes. | Learners and everyday users |
| Child / family member | A standard account with parental controls such as screen-time limits and website filters (Microsoft Family Safety). | Young children at home |
| Guest (older Windows versions) | Temporary, very limited access; no personal files are kept. Removed from Windows 10 and 11. | Visitors |
In Windows 11, accounts are managed in **Settings › Accounts › Other users** (or **Family**). When a standard user tries to make a system change, **User Account Control (UAC)** asks for an administrator password.
## Permission levels for files and folders
**Permissions** are rules that state who may do what with a file or folder. On Windows (NTFS drives), right-click a file or folder › **Properties › Security** tab to see them.
| **Permission** | **Allows the user to…** |
|---|---|
| Full control | do everything, including change permissions and take ownership |
| Modify | read, change and delete the file or folder |
| Read & execute | view the contents and run programs |
| List folder contents | see the names of the files inside a folder |
| Read | open and view, but not change |
| Write | add new files or change contents |

pages.title: File Management, Users and Accounts (continued)
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Worked example — Permissions in the school lab**
A Class_Notes folder on the lab server gives learners **Read** permission (they can open notes but not delete them), while the teacher has **Full control**. A Submissions folder gives learners **Write** permission so they can hand in work without seeing each other’s files.
> 💻 **Practical session — Organise your own files**
1. Create a folder structure like the one shown in this lesson in your Documents folder, using your own name and subjects.
2. Turn on **File name extensions**. Create a Word file, an Excel file and a Notepad text file, and save each in the correct folder with a meaningful name. Note each extension.
3. Right-click your Computing folder › **Properties › Security**. List the users and their permissions.
4. Open **Settings › Accounts › Your info** and identify whether your account is an Administrator or Standard account.

pages.title: Review: written and practical tasks
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. State **four** features of fourth-generation computers.
2. Explain the functions of the Control Unit, ALU and registers in a processor.
3. Distinguish between manual and automatic input devices, giving **two** examples of each.
4. Give **two** advantages and **two** disadvantages of using a touchscreen.
5. Describe how a data projector differs from a multimedia projector.
6. Explain what is meant by disk caching and why it improves performance.
7. Copy and complete: CD-R is ______ while CD-RW is ______.
8. What is a file extension? Why is it useful to make extensions visible?
9. Explain the difference between an Administrator and a Standard user account.
## Practical tasks
1. Set up the class projector, connect a laptop and use **Windows + P** to duplicate the display.
2. Create a folder structure for all your B7 subjects. Save at least one file in each folder using the naming conventions you have learnt.
3. Open three programs and demonstrate taskbar thumbnail previews and peeking to your partner.
